label: theo:1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:1}
 Let $\mathcal{L} \subset \mathcal{M}_G$ be a visible Lagrangian, such that $\mathcal{B}'=\mathrm{Hit}(\mathcal{L}) \subsetneq \mathcal{B}_G$ and $\mathcal{B}' \cap \mathcal{B}^\mathrm{reg}_G \neq \varnothing$. Let $s\colon \mathcal{B}' \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$ be a section of $\mathrm{Hit}\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{\mathcal{L}}$. The fiber-wise Fourier--Mukai transform of the structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{L}$ is supported on a holomorphic symplectic subvariety $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{L},s} \subset \mathcal{M}_{G^{\rm L}}$ such that $\mathrm{Hit}\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{\mathcal{I}}\colon \mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{L},s} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}'$ is an algebraically completely integrable system.

label: theo:intro:1-dim_examples
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:intro:1-dim_examples}
 Let $q \in H^0\bigl(X,K_X^2\bigr)$ be a quadratic differential with simple zeros only. Then there exists a visible Lagrangian
 \[ \mathcal{L} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}'=\{t q \mid t \in \mathbb{C}\} \subset \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X)
 \]
 if and only if $(X,q)$ is a pillowcase cover.

label: theo:intro_3
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:intro_3}
 There exist infinitely many genera $g$, such that there exists a~Riemann surface~$X$ of genus~$g$ with two quadratic differentials $q_1$, $q_2$ with simple zeros only, such that $(X,q_i)$ are pillowcase covers and $q_1$, $q_2$ are not related by pullback along an automorphism of~$X$.

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $(X,q)$ be a uniform pillowcase cover with simple zeros only and $\mathcal{L} \rightarrow \mathbb{C} q$ the visible Lagrangian of Theorem~{\rm \ref{theo:intro:1-dim_examples}}. Then the associated subintegrable system $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{PGL}(2,\mathbb{C})}$ of Theorem~{\rm \ref{theo:1}} is a hyperholomorphic subvariety.

label: defi:integrable_system
title: Definition
body_md: \label{defi:integrable_system} A completely integrable system is a holomorphic symplectic manifold $(M,\Omega)$ together with a proper flat morphism $H\colon M \rightarrow B$ to a complex manifold $B$, such that on the complement $B\setminus S$ of some proper closed subvariety $S$ the fibers of $H$ are complex Lagrangian tori. It~is called algebraically completely integrable, if the Lagrangian tori are endowed with continuously varying polarizations $\rho_b \in H^{(1,1)}(M_b) \cap H^2(M_b,\mathbb{Z})$, i.e., they are abelian varieties.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: An integral affine structure on a smooth manifold $B$ is a torsion-free flat connection $\nabla$ on the tangent bundle $TB$ together with a $\nabla$-covariant sublattice $\Lambda \subset TB$ of maximal rank. A~submanifold $B' \subset B$ is called rational with respect to the integral affine structure, if for all $b \in B'$ the tangent space $T_bB'$ is generated by a rational linear combination of elements of~$\Lambda_b$.

label: def:visible-lagrangians
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:visible-lagrangians}
Let $H\colon M \rightarrow B$ be a completely integrable system. A Lagrangian subvariety $\mathcal{L} \subset M$ is called \textit{visible}, if it is closed and $H\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{\mathcal{L}}\colon \mathcal{L} \rightarrow B$ factors as $H\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{\mathcal{L}}=f \circ g$, where $f\colon B' \rightarrow B$ is an embedding of a proper subvariety $B'$ such that $g\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{B'\setminus S'}\colon \mathcal{L}\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{B'\setminus S'} \rightarrow B'\setminus S'$ is a smooth fiber bundle on the complement of some proper subvariety $S' \subsetneq B'$.

label: theo:visible_Lagr
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{theo:visible_Lagr} Let $H\colon M \rightarrow B$ be a completely integrable system and $\mathcal{L} \rightarrow B' \subsetneq B$ a visible Lagrangian with $B'^\mathrm{reg} \subset B^\mathrm{reg}$. Then at each smooth point $b \in B'^\mathrm{reg}$ the subvariety $B'$ is rational with respect to the integral affine structure on $B^\mathrm{reg}$ and for $b \in B'^\mathrm{reg}$ the fiber $\mathcal{L}_b$ is a union of complex tori generated by the invariant vector fields $T_bB'^\perp \subset V_bM$.

title: \proofname
body_md: The original statement gives the isomorphism with values in $H^0(\Sigma_{\underline{a}},\pi^*K_X^n)$. We have the isomorphism of sheaves $K_{\Sigma_{\underline{a}}} \rightarrow \pi^*K_X^n$ given by $ \phi \mapsto \phi s_B\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_U$ for $\phi \in K_{\Sigma_{\underline{a}}}\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_U$. This is well defined by the following: Let $(U,w)$ a coordinate disc centered at $y \in \Sigma$, such that $\pi\colon U \rightarrow \pi(U)$, $w \mapsto z=w^b$ with $b \geq 1$. Then $s_B\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_U= b w^{b-1} (\pi^* \mathrm{d} z)^{n-1}$. Hence, $\phi \cdot s_B(U)=f \mathrm{d} w \cdot b w^{b-1} (\pi^* \mathrm{d} z)^{n-1}=f (\pi^* \mathrm{d} z)^{n}$, where we used that $\pi^* \mathrm{d} z= b w^{b-1} \mathrm{d} w$. Composing Baraglia's isomorphism \cite[Proposition~3.4]{Baraglia} with the inverse of the above defines the asserted isomorphism~$t$.\looseness=1

label: prop:criterion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:criterion} A closed subvariety $\mathcal{L} \subset \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$ over a proper subvariety $\mathcal{B}' \subsetneq \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$ with $\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg} \subset \mathcal{B}^\mathrm{reg}$ and connected fibers is a visible Lagrangian if and only if
 \begin{itemize}\itemsep=0pt
 \item[$(i)$] There exists an abelian subscheme $A \subset \mathrm{Jac}\bigl(\Sigma/\mathcal{B}_G^\mathrm{reg}\bigr) \: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{B'^\mathrm{reg}}$ over $\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$, such that $\mathcal{L}$ is an $A$-torsor.
 \item[$(ii)$] The relative tangent bundle $T_{A/\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}} \subset T_{\mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma)/\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}}$ is the kernel of the map
 \[ T_{\mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma)/\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}} \cong R^1\pi_*\mathcal{O}_\Sigma \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{\dim \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}}
 \]
 defined by evaluating on the image of
 \[ T\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg} \rightarrow R^0\pi_*K_\Sigma, \qquad X \mapsto t(X)
 \]
 using the Serre pairing on $\Sigma$. Here $t$ was defined in Proposition~{\rm \ref{prop:Baraglia}}.
 \end{itemize}

title: \proofname
body_md: By Theorem~\ref{theo:visible_Lagr}, fibers of $\mathcal{L} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$ are complex subtori in the Hitchin fiber. Hence, using a local section $s\colon U \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$ on an open $U \subset \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$, we can identify the fibers with an abelian subscheme of $A \rightarrow \mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma/\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg})$. Condition (ii) is the family version of Theorem~\ref{theo:visible_Lagr} reformulated by using the observations about the holomorphic symplectic form on $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$ in the previous paragraph. Conversely, condition (ii) is equivalent to the restriction of the symplectic form of~$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$ to be zero on the tangent bundle to $\mathcal{L}$. Hence, $\mathcal{L}$ is a Lagrangian.

label: theo:FM
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{theo:FM} Let $\mathcal{L} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}'\subset \mathcal{B}_{G}$ be a visible Lagrangian in $\mathcal{M}_G$ with $\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg} \subset \mathcal{B}^\mathrm{reg}$, connected fibers and a section $s\colon \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$. We identify the $G$- $($resp.\ $G^{\rm L}$-$)$ Hitchin system over $\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$ with the abelian schemes using the section~$s$ $($resp.\ $s'=\delta \circ s)$. Then the fiber-wise Fourier--Mukai transform of the structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{L}}$ over $\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$ is the structure sheaf of the holomorphic symplectic subvariety $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{M}_{G^{\rm L}}$ defined in Theorem~{\rm \ref{theo:subintegrable_syst}}.

title: \proofname
body_md:
Let $\underline{a} \in \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$ and denote by $P=\mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})$. As in the previous proof we use the section $s$ to obtain the exact sequences of abelian varieties
 \[ 0 \rightarrow A \rightarrow P \rightarrow Q \rightarrow 0 \quad (\ref{eq:exact_sequ}) \qquad \mathrm{and} \qquad 0 \rightarrow Q^\vee \rightarrow P^\vee \rightarrow A^\vee \rightarrow 0 \quad (\ref{eq:dual_exact_sequ}).
 \]
 We use the symmetric Fourier--Mukai transform introduced in~\cite{Schnell}. More precisely, we are going to use Proposition~1.6 therein. We denote by $\mathcal{P} \rightarrow P \times P^\vee$ the Poincar\'e bundle. Then the symmetric Fourier--Mukai transform is defined by
 \[ \operatorname{SFM}_P\colon \ D^b(P) \rightarrow D^b\bigl(P^\vee\bigr), \qquad \operatorname{FM}_{\mathcal{P}} \circ \Delta_P,
 \]
 where $\Delta_P=\mathrm{Hom}(\cdot,\omega_P[\dim P])$ is the Serre duality functor. First we have to show that $\mathcal{O}_A$ is a GV-sheaf. By \cite[Definition~3.1]{PareschiPopa}, this means that the support loci
 \[ \bigl\{ \xi \in P^\vee \mid H^i\bigl(P,\iota_*\mathcal{O}_A \otimes \mathcal{P}_\xi^{-1}\bigr)\neq 0 \bigr\}
 \]
 have codimension $\geq i$ for all $i$. Let $\xi \in P^\vee$. We have
 \[ H^i\bigl(P,\iota_*\mathcal{O}_A \otimes \mathcal{P}_\xi^{-1}\bigr)=H^i\bigl(A,\mathcal{P}_\xi^{-1}\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{A}\bigr).
 \]
 It is zero for $i > \dim A$. For $i \leq \dim A$, it is non-zero if and only if $\mathcal{P}_\xi^{-1} \: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_A$ is trivial. Hence, if and only if $\xi \in Q^\vee$. Therefore, the support loci satisfy the dimension condition and $\iota_*\mathcal{O}_A$ is a GV sheaf on $P$. In particular, it is WIT -- that is $\operatorname{SFM}_P(\mathcal{O}_A)$ is a sheaf -- by \cite[Proposition~3.2]{PareschiPopa}.

 The symmetric Fourier--Mukai transform on $A$ has the property
 \begin{align} \label{eq:FM_of_point} \operatorname{SFM}_A(\mathcal{O}_A)=\mathbb{C}_0, \qquad \operatorname{SFM}_{A^\vee}(\mathbb{C}_0) = \mathcal{O}_{A},
 \end{align}
 where $\mathbb{C}_0$ is the skyscraper sheaf of length $1$ at $0 \in P^\vee$. Now \cite[Proposition~1.6]{Schnell} states that if a sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ is GV on $A$ and $\iota_*\mathcal{F}$ is GV on $P$, then
 \[ \operatorname{SFM}_P(\iota_*\mathcal{F})=\bigl(\iota^\vee\bigr)^*\operatorname{SFM}_A(\mathcal{F}).
 \]
 By~(\ref{eq:FM_of_point}), this yields $\operatorname{SFM}_P(\mathcal{O}_A)=\mathcal{O}_{Q^\vee}$.

label: rema:GL
title: Remark
body_md: \label{rema:GL} The above arguments similarly work for the case of $G=G^{\rm L}=\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})$. Here the Hitchin system restricted to \smash{$\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}^{\mathrm{reg}}$} is a torsor over the abelian scheme \smash{$\mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma) \rightarrow \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}^{\mathrm{reg}}$}, which is self-dual due to the principal polarization of the Jacobians. Hence, again given a visible Lagrangian with connected fibers together with a section we obtain a holomorphic symplectic submanifold $\mathcal{I}$ by the arguments of the proof of Theorem~\ref{theo:subintegrable_syst}. Furthermore, the arguments in the proof of Theorem~\ref{theo:FM} work for the structure sheaf of any abelian subvariety of an abelian variety.

label: theo:Lagr_SL_in_GL
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{theo:Lagr_SL_in_GL} Let $\mathcal{B}'=\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})}(X) \subset \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$ with \smash{$\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}=\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$}. Then we can act by the trivial torsor $\mathrm{Jac}(X) \times \mathcal{B}'$ on the Hitchin section by tensoring the underlying bundle. The orbit defines a visible Lagrangian $\mathcal{L} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}'$. The fiber-wise Fourier--Mukai transform of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{L}}$ over $\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$ is supported on the moduli space of~$\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})$-Higgs bundles $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})} \subset \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$.

label: eq:sequence_Jac_Prym
title: \proofname
body_md:
Tensoring with a line bundle preserves stability. Hence $\mathcal{L}$ is well defined.
 The Hitchin fiber over $\underline{a} \in \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$ reflects the splitting of the differentials on $\Sigma$ by the isomorphism
\[ \mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})= \pi^*\mathrm{Jac}(X) \times \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})/\pi^*\mathrm{Jac}(X)[n],
\] where $\pi^*\mathrm{Jac}(X)[n]$ acts diagonally (see Mumford \cite{Mumford}). In particular, we have an exact sequence of abelian schemes over $\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$
\begin{align} 0 \rightarrow \mathrm{Jac}(X) \times \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg} \xrightarrow{\iota} \mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma/\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma/\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg})/ \pi^* \mathrm{Jac}(X)[n] \rightarrow 0. \label{eq:sequence_Jac_Prym}
\end{align}
 As explained in Section~\ref{sec:prel-Hitchin_syst}, the holomorphic symplectic form on \smash{$\mathrm{Hit}^{-1}\bigl(\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}\bigr) \subset \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$} restricts to the Serre pairing between the tangent space of the base identified with $H^0({\Sigma_{\underline{a}}},K_{\Sigma_{\underline{a}}})$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:Baraglia} and the tangent space to the fibers $H^1({\Sigma_{\underline{a}}}, \mathcal{O}_{\Sigma_{\underline{a}}})$. With respect to this pairing, we have
 \[ H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)^\perp=H^0({\Sigma_{\underline{a}}},K_{\Sigma_{\underline{a}}})^-.
 \]
 The subtorsor $\mathcal{L} \subset \mathrm{Hit}^{-1}(\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg})$ that is defined by the action of $\mathrm{Jac}(X) \times \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$ on the Hitchin section has vertical tangent bundle $H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ and the tangent space to the $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})$ Hitchin base are identified with $H^0(\Sigma_{\underline{a}},K_{\Sigma_{\underline{a}}})^-$. Therefore, $\mathcal{L}$ is a visible Lagrangian.

 By Theorem~\ref{theo:FM}, the fiber-wise Fourier--Mukai transform of the structure sheaf of $\mathcal{L}$ over $\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$ is supported on torsor over the abelian scheme that is dual to quotient in the exact sequence~(\ref{eq:sequence_Jac_Prym}). That is the abelian scheme \smash{$\mathrm{Prym}\bigl(\Sigma/ \mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})}\bigr)$}. The closure of this locus is the moduli space of $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})$-Higgs bundles.

label: theo:Lagr_SL_in_GL_multisection
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{theo:Lagr_SL_in_GL_multisection} Let $\mathcal{B}'=\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})} \subset \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb{C})}$ with \smash{$\mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}=\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}$}. We can act by the trivial torsor $\mathrm{Jac}(X) \times \mathcal{B}'$ on $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}'$ by tensoring. The orbit defines a visible Lagrangian $\mathcal{L} \rightarrow \mathcal{B}'$. For $\underline{a} \in \mathcal{B}'^\mathrm{reg}$, the fiber-wise Fourier--Mukai transform of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{L}_{\underline{a}}}$ is supported on $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})} \subset \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb{C})}$ and given by a flat vector bundle of rank $6g-6$ on $\mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})$.
head: environment

title: \proofname
body_md:
Let $U \subset \mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}$ open, such that there exist sections
 \[ s_1=s_H, s_2, \dots, s_{6g-6}\colon \ U \rightarrow \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}
 \]
 such that $\mathrm{Hit}^{-1}(U) \cap \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})} = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{6g-6} s_i(U)$. Then the orbit of each $s_i(U)$ under tensoring with line bundles in $\mathrm{Jac}(X)$ is Lagrangian by the previous proof. Hence, $\mathcal{L}$ defines a visible Lagrangians.

 We identify the Hitchin fibers with the abelian scheme $\mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma)$ using the Hitchin section~$s_1$. Fix $\underline{a} \in U$ and define $l_i = (s_1-s_i)(\underline{a}) \in \mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})$. Recall the exact sequence of abelian schemes~(\ref{eq:sequence_Jac_Prym}). We have
 \[ \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{L}_{\underline{a}}} = \bigoplus\limits_{i=1}^{6g-6} t^*_{l_i} \iota_* \mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Jac}(X)},
 \] where $t_{l_i}$ denotes the translation by $l_i$ on $\mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})$. Let $J=\mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})$ and $\mathcal{P} \rightarrow J \times J$ the Poincar\'e bundle. Using the relation between tensor product and translations under Fourier--Mukai transform (see \cite{Schnell}), we obtain
 \begin{align*} \operatorname{SFM}_{J}(t^*_{l_i} \iota_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Jac}(X)}) = \mathcal{P}_{l_i} \otimes \operatorname{SFM}_{J}(\iota_* \mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Jac}(X)})= \mathcal{P}_{l_i} \otimes \bigl(\iota^\vee\bigr)^* \mathbb{C}_0 = \mathcal{P}_{l_i} \otimes \mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})}.
 \end{align*}
 The right hand side defines a flat line bundle on $\mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}})$. The Fourier--Mukai of the structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{L}_{\underline{a}}}$ is the direct sum of all these flat line bundles.

title: Definition
body_md: A translation surface $(\Sigma, \lambda)$ is parallelogram-tiled if and only if there exists a branched cover $p\colon \Sigma \rightarrow E$ branched over one point, such that $\lambda=p^*\omega$ for some abelian differential $\omega$ on $E$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A half-translation surface $(X,q)$ is called pillowcase cover if there exists a cover $ \check{p}\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$ branched over $D=(0,1,\infty,x)$, such that $q= \check{p}^*\eta$ for a quadratic differential $\eta$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ with simple poles at~$D$.
head: environment

label: lemm:pillow
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{lemm:pillow} Let $(X,q)$ be a half-trans\-lation surface. The canonical cover $(\Sigma,\lambda)$ is a para\-llelo\-gram-tiled surface if and only if the quadratic differential is a pillowcase cover.
head: environment

title: \proofname
body_md:
Starting from a pillowcase cover as above, we have the following diagram:
\[	\begin{tikzcd}
		& (\Sigma,\lambda) \ar[rd,"p",dashed] \ar[ld,"\pi" above, "\mod J" right]& \\ (X,q) \ar[rd,"\check{p}"] & & (E, \omega) \ar[ld,"2:1"] \\ & \bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,\eta\bigr) &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
and want to show that there exist the dashed arrow $p\colon \Sigma \rightarrow E$, such that the diagram commutes. Away from the singularities of the flat structure associated with $(X,q)$ a point on $\Sigma$ corresponds to a choice of a (local) square of~$q$. This corresponds to a choice of a local square root of $\eta$ under the covering map to $\mathbb{P}^1$. Hence, there is a induced map $p\colon \Sigma\setminus Z(\lambda) \rightarrow E \setminus Z(\omega)$ such that $p^*\omega=\lambda$.
The map $p$ uniquely extends to a map of Riemann surfaces $\Sigma \rightarrow E$. A zero $x \in X$ of $q$ of order $k\geq 0$ corresponds to a $(k+2):1$-branch point of $\check{p}$. Hence, the map can be extended to $p\colon \Sigma \rightarrow E$ by gluing in a $k:1$ ramification point, if $k$ is odd and a $\frac{k}{2}:1$ ramification point, if~$k$ is even, at $y \in \pi^{-1}(x)$.
 By construction the relation of the differentials persists under this extension. Taking the quotient of $E$ by two-torsion points we obtain a map $(\Sigma,\lambda) \rightarrow E/E[2]$, branched over one point such that $\lambda$ is the pullback of a differential on~$E$. Hence, it is a parallelogram-tiled surface.

For the converse, we start with the configuration
\[ 	\begin{tikzcd}
		& (\Sigma,\lambda) \ar[rd,"p"] \ar[ld,"\pi" above left, "\mod J" right]& \\ (X,q) & & (E, \omega).
	\end{tikzcd}
\]
The differential $\lambda$ is anti-symmetric with respect to an involution~$J$. In particular, $J$ sends singularities of the flat structure to singularities of the same type, saddle connections to saddle connections and hence squares to squares. Hence, it descends to the elliptic curve $(E,\omega)$ to the reflection in the two torsion points of~$E$. The quotient is the pillowcase surface as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:Pillowcase}. In particular, there is an induced map $\check{p}\colon \Sigma/J=X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$, such that $q=\check{p}^*\eta$.

title: Remark
body_md: The proof of the previous lemma shows that one can always assume the pillowcase cover to be non-simply branched over only one point on $\mathbb{P}^1$. This can be achieved by taking the quotient by the order four automorphism of $\mathbb{P}^1$ that permutes the four marked points preserving the cross-ratio.

label: defi:uniform_pillow_cover
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defi:uniform_pillow_cover}
	We call a pillowcase cover $(X,q)$ \emph{uniform} if every fiber of $\check{p}\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$ over $y \in D$ consists of ramification points of the same ramification index~$i$.

title: Definition
body_md:
We call a Riemann surface $X$ with quadratic differentials $q_1,\dots,q_n$ as above a~\emph{$n$-fold pillowcase cover}.
	We call a $n$-fold pillowcase cover a \emph{multifold pillowcase cover} if $n \geq 2$.

label: theo:multifold_pillow
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:multifold_pillow}
	For infinitely many genera $g$, there exist multifold uniform pillowcase covers with simple zeros only.
head: environment

title: \proofname
body_md:
Assume that we know a single multifold uniform pillowcase cover $X$ with simple zeros only of some genus $g \geq 2$.
	Let $q_1, \dots, q_n$ be the corresponding quadratic differentials.
	Then we can obtain examples in infinitely many genera by taking unramified coverings $f\colon \widehat X \rightarrow X$ in different degrees and the differentials $\widehat q_i = f^* q_i$.

We will provide explicit examples in the following.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the group $\mathrm{GL}(2,F_3)$ of order $48$ and let $f\colon X\rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$ be the $\mathrm{GL}(2, F_3)$-cover branched above three points with monodromy datum
\[
	\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
	\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
	\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The orders of the matrices are $8$, $2$ and $6$, and the genus of $X$ is $2$.
The group $\mathrm{GL}(2,F_3)$ has $12$ subgroups of order $6$ which we denote by $H_1, \dots, H_{12}$.
For each such subgroup the quotient~$X/H_i$ is of genus $0$, and the quotient map $g_i\colon X \rightarrow X/H_i$ is branched above four points with ramification orders~$2$ and~$3$.
Let~$\eta_i$ denote the quadratic differential on $X/H_i$ of type~$(-1^4)$ whose simple poles are supported at the branch points of~$g_i$.
The pullback $q_i := g_i^*\eta_i$ is a~uniform pillowcase cover with simple zeros only on $X$.
We claim that the vanishing loci of the differentials~$q_i$ are pairwise different. This is a very explicit but lengthy computation which is left to the reader.
In particular, $X$~is a $12$-fold uniform pillowcase cover with simple zeros only.

name: genus 2

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the group $\mathrm{SL}(3,F_2)$ of order $168$ and let $f\colon X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^1$ be the $\mathrm{SL}(3,F_2)$-cover branched above three points with monodromy datum
\[
	\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
	\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
	\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The orders of the matrices are $2$, $3$ and $7$. The Riemann surface $X$ is the Klein quartic and has genus $3$.
The group $\mathrm{SL}(3,F_2)$ has $14$ subgroups of order~$24$, and as in the previous example each of those subgroups gives rise to a uniform pillowcase covers with simple zeros only.
In particular, $X$ is a $14$-fold uniform pillowcase cover with simple zeros only.

Let $G := A_4 \times \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$.

Let $f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$ be the $G$-cover branched above three points with monodromy datum $\bigl(bc, a^2c^2, ab\bigr)$.
The genus of~$X$ is~$4$.

Consider the two intermediate covers $A_1 := X/H_1$ and $A_2 := X/H_2$, both of genus $0$.
We~define the two differentials $q_1$ and $q_2$ on $X$ as in the previous examples.

In this example, it is relatively easy to see that the differentials $q_1$ and $q_2$ are non-isomorphic.
For this, it is convenient to consider the respective canonical covers $(\Sigma_i, \lambda_i)$ of~$(X, q_i)$.

label: theo:visi_Lagr_over_line
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{theo:visi_Lagr_over_line} Let \smash{$\underline{a}=(0,\dots,0,a_n) \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})}^\mathrm{reg}$}. Then there exists a visible Lagrangian over~$\mathbb{C} \underline{a}$, if and only if the spectral curve with its abelian differential $(\Sigma,\lambda)$ is parallelogram-tiled.
head: environment

label: one-form
title: \proofname
body_md:
First, assume there exists a visible Lagrangian over~$\mathbb{C}\underline{a}$. Let $(\Sigma,\lambda)$ be the spectral curve to $\underline{a}$. Then, by Proposition~\ref{prop:criterion}, there is an exact sequence of abelian varieties
 \[ 0 \rightarrow A \rightarrow \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma_{\underline{a}}) \xrightarrow{\psi} E \rightarrow 0.
 \]
 Here $A$ is of codimension $1$ and $E$ is an elliptic curve. Under the assumption on $\underline{a}$, the spectral curve is $\mathbb{Z}_n$-Galois and $s_B=\lambda^{n-1}$ (up to a constant). Hence, the map $t$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:Baraglia} becomes
 \[ t\colon \ \bigoplus\limits_{i=2}^n H^0(X,K_X^i) \rightarrow H^0(\Sigma,K_\Sigma), \qquad \sum\limits_{i=2}^n \alpha_i X_i \mapsto \sum\limits_{i=2}^n \alpha_i \frac{\pi^*X_i}{\lambda^{i-1}}.
 \] In particular, the tangent vector $X_n=a_n$ is mapped to $\frac{\pi^*a_n}{\lambda^{n-1}}=\lambda$.
 Hence, the differential of the map $\psi$ can explicitly be written as
 \begin{align} \mathrm{d} \psi\colon \ H^1(\Sigma, \mathcal{O}_\Sigma)^- \rightarrow T_0E, \qquad \alpha \mapsto c \int_\Sigma \alpha \wedge \lambda. \label{one-form}
 \end{align}
 Therefore, $\psi$ is given by $D=\sum a_i y_i \mapsto \sum a_i\int_{y_0}^{y_i} \lambda$ up to the choice of a point $y_0 \in \Sigma$. Denote by $\sigma$ a generator of the $\mathbb{Z}_n$ action on $\Sigma$. We want show that the composition $\psi \circ \mathrm{AP}$ with the Abel--Prym map
 \[ \mathrm{AP}\colon \ \Sigma \rightarrow \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma), \qquad y \mapsto \mathcal{O}(y-\sigma y)
 \]
 is a branched covering $p\colon \Sigma \rightarrow E$. Clearly, $\mathrm{AP}$ identifies all ramification points of $\pi\colon \Sigma \rightarrow X$. If~$\Sigma$ is not hyperelliptic, it is easy to see that these are the only points on $\Sigma$ that are identified. The spectral curve $\Sigma$ is never hyperelliptic by \cite[Lemma~4.1]{Baraglia}. By definition, $\sigma^*\lambda=\xi_n \lambda$ for some primitive $n$-th root of unity $\xi_n$. This implies that the differential of the composition $\psi \circ \mathrm{AP}$ is $(1-\xi) \lambda$. Hence, the differential of the composition is injective away from the ramification points of $\Sigma \rightarrow X$. In particular, $p=\psi \circ \mathrm{AP}\colon \Sigma \rightarrow E$ is a proper holomorphic map ramified at $Z(\lambda)$ over $0 \in E$. Furthermore, $\lambda$ considered as abelian differential has an order $n$ zero at each branch point and hence the points in $Z(\lambda)$ are $n+1:1$ ramifications. In particular, the pullback of an abelian differential~$\omega$ on~$E$ has the same divisor as~$\lambda$ and we can find a~specific~$\omega$ with $p^*\omega=\lambda$. Therefore, $(\Sigma,\lambda)$ is parallelogram-tiled.

 For the converse, let \smash{$\underline{a}=(0,\dots,0,a_n) \in \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})}^\mathrm{reg}$}, such that $(\Sigma,\lambda)$ is paralle\-lo\-gram-tiled, i.e., there is a covering $p\colon \Sigma \rightarrow E$, such that $\lambda=p^*\omega$ for some abelian differential $\omega$ on~$E$. The covering~$p$ induces a Norm map
 \[ \mathrm{Nm}_E\colon \ \mathrm{Jac}(\Sigma) \rightarrow E, \qquad D=\sum a_iy_i \mapsto \sum a_i \int_{y_0}^{y_i} \lambda.
 \] The restriction to $\mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma)$ defines the desired map
 \[ \psi=\mathrm{Nm}_E \: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{\mathrm{Prym}}\colon \ \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma) \rightarrow E.
 \] Let $D=(n-1)y - \sigma y - \dots - \sigma^{n-1}y$. Then $D \in \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma)$ and $\mathrm{Nm}_E(D)= n \mathrm{Nm}_E(y)$. Hence, $\psi$~surjects onto $E$ being a divisible group. Its differential is the map~\eqref{one-form}. As $\Sigma$ does not change, when multiplying $q$ with a scalar, we can define an abelian subscheme $\mathrm{ker}(\psi) \subset \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma/\mathbb{C}^\times q)$ that satisfies the criterion of Proposition~\ref{prop:criterion}. To obtain a visible Lagrangian over~$\mathbb{C} q$, we can act with the abelian scheme $\mathrm{ker}(\psi)$ on any section of $\mathrm{Hit} \: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{\mathbb{C} \underline{a}}$. To obtain a concrete example, we~may choose the Hitchin section.

label: prop:Hausel_toy
title: Proposition
body_md: \label{prop:Hausel_toy} The subvariety $\mathcal{I}_q \!\subset\! \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{PSL}(n,\mathbb{C})}$ is birational to Hausel's toy model~$\mathcal{M}_\mathrm{toy}$.
head: environment

title: \proofname
body_md:
Hausel's toy model is constructed as an elliptic surface as follows. Take $\bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4\bigr)$ and consider the elliptic curve $E \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1$, which is the canonical cover of the pillowcase with involution~$\tau$. Let further $\tau'$ be the involution $-1\colon \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$. Consider $M=E \times \mathbb{C}/(\tau \times \tau')$. This orbifold has 4 $\mathbb{Z}_2$-points $\widehat{p}_i \times 0$. The projection to the second factor induces the map $M \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, $(x,y) \mapsto y^2 $ with generic fiber $E$. Blowing up the 4~orbifold points, we obtain a smooth surface~-- the toy model $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{toy}}$.

 The subintegrable system $\mathcal{I}_q$ associated to $\mathcal{B}'=\mathbb{C} q$ for a pillowcase cover $(X,q)$ is an elliptic fibration over $\mathbb{C}^\times q \subset \mathcal{B}'$. The modulus of the elliptic curve is constant and determined by the four points $p_1,\dots,p_4$ on the pillowcase. As for Hausel's toy model, the monodromy around $0 \in \mathbb{C} q$ is given by $-1$. In fact, if we scale our quadratic differential with $e^{i\phi}$, the abelian differential is multiplied by $e^{i\frac12 \phi}$. This defines an isomorphism between $M\setminus{\{y=0\}}$ and $\mathcal{I}_q \: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{\mathbb{C}^\times q}$.

label: theo:Theta
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:Theta}
 Let $(X,q)$ be a uniform pillowcase cover with simple zeros only. We define so-called compatible parabolic weights at $y \in D$ of ramification index $i$ by \smash{$\bigl(\alpha_0=\frac{i+1}{i+2}, \alpha_1=\frac{1}{i+2}\bigr)$}. Let $\mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}\bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,D\bigr)$ be the moduli space of strongly parabolic Higgs bundles on $\bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,D\bigr)$ with compatible parabolic weights. Then there exists a holomorphic map
 \[ \Theta\colon \ \mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}\bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,D\bigr) \rightarrow \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X)
 \] such that
 \begin{itemize}\itemsep=0pt
 \item[$(i)$] it maps the Hitchin section of $\mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$ to the Hitchin section of $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X)$ restricted to $\mathbb{C} q$.
 \item[$(ii)$] for all $c \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, it makes the following diagram commute
 \[ \begin{tikzcd} E \ar[r,"p^*"]\ar[d,"\cong"] & \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma_q) \ar[d,"\cong"] \\
 \mathrm{Hit}^{-1}(c\eta) \ar[r,"\Theta"] & \mathrm{Hit}^{-1}(cq),
 \end{tikzcd} \]
 where we used the Hitchin section to identify the corresponding Hitchin fibers with abelian varieties.
 \item[$(iii)$] $\Theta$ can be promoted to a morphism of hermitian Higgs bundles, such that solutions to the Hitchin equation on \smash{$\bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,D\bigr)$} are mapped to solutions to the Hitchin equation on~$X$.
 \end{itemize}
head: environment

title: \proofname
body_md:
Recall the square of coverings of Figure~\ref{fig:square-of-covers}. The morphism $\Theta$ is given by a Hecke modified pullback along $\check{p}$. Let $(\mathcal{E},\Phi) \in \mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$. First define
 \[ (\mathcal{E}',\Phi')= \bigl(\check{p}^*(\mathcal{E}\otimes\mathcal{O}(3))\otimes K_X^{-\frac12}, \check{p}^*\Phi\bigr).
 \]
 This is a meromorphic Higgs bundle on $X$ with $\mathrm{tr}(\Phi')=0$. By assumption of $q$ having simple zeros only all points in $\check{p}^{-1}(D)$ are ramification points of $\check{p}$, which are $2:1$ or $3:1$. Let $R_i \in \mathrm{Div}^+(X)$ be the divisor that has weight $1$ at the branch points that are $(i+1):1$ and $R=R_1 +R_2$. The pullback of the quasi-parabolic structure defines a quasi-parabolic structure on $\mathcal{E}'$ at $R$ given by $\mathcal{E}'_{x,1}:=\check{p}^*\mathcal{E}_{\check{p}x,1} \subset \mathcal{E}_{x}$. Now we define a Hecke modification
 \[ 0 \rightarrow \bigl(\hat{\mathcal{E}},\hat{\Phi}\bigr) \rightarrow (\mathcal{E}',\Phi') \rightarrow \bigoplus_{x \in \mathrm{supp} R} \mathcal{E}'_{x}/\mathcal{E}'_{x,1} \rightarrow 0.
 \]
 Then the map $\Theta$ is defined as
 $\Theta\colon (\mathcal{E},\Phi) \mapsto (\hat{\mathcal{E}},\hat{\Phi})$.

 \begin{figure}[h]
$$
 \begin{tikzcd}
	& (\Sigma,\lambda) \ar[rd,"p"] \ar[ld,"\pi" above]& \\ (X,q) \ar[rd,"\check{p}"] & & (E, \omega) \ar[ld,"\check{\pi}"] \\ & \bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,\eta\bigr) &
 \end{tikzcd}\vspace{-3mm}
$$
 \caption{Square of coverings associated to a pillowcase.}\label{fig:square-of-covers}
 \end{figure}

 \textit{Well-definedness:} First, we have to show that $\Theta$ is well defined. We have
 \[ \check{p}^*\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-2)=\check{p}^*K_{\mathbb{P}^1}=K_X(-R_1-2R_2)
 \]
 and $\mathrm{div}(q)=R_2$. Hence, the determinant of $E'$ computes to
 \[ \det(\mathcal{E}')=\check{p}^*\mathcal{O}(2) \otimes K_X^{-1}=K_X^{-2}(R_1+2R_2)=\mathcal{O}(R_1+R_2).
 \]
 Therefore, the determinant of $\hat{\mathcal{E}}$ is $\det\bigl(\hat{\mathcal{E}}\bigr)=\det(\mathcal{E}')(-R_1-R_2)=\mathcal{O}_X$.

 To show that the Higgs field $\hat{\Phi}$ is holomorphic we do a local computation. Locally at each $y \in D$, we can find a frame $s_1$, $s_2$ of $\mathcal{E}$ adapted to the parabolic structure such that
 \begin{align} \Phi= \begin{pmatrix} \phi_0(z) \mathrm{d} z & \phi_1(z) \dfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{z} \vspace{1mm}\\ \phi_2(z) \mathrm{d} z & -\phi_0(z) \mathrm{d} z \end{pmatrix}.
 \label{eq:local-model-Phi}
 \end{align}
 and $\mathcal{E}_{y,1}=\langle s_1\: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_{y} \rangle$. Hence, at all ramification points $x \in \check{p}^{-1}D$ the pullback has the form
 \begin{align} \label{eq:local-model-Phi'}
 \check{p}^* \Phi= \begin{pmatrix} \phi_0\bigl(w^k\bigr) w^{k-1} \mathrm{d} w & \phi_1\bigl(w^k\bigr) \dfrac{ \mathrm{d} w}{w} \vspace{1mm}\\ \phi_2\bigl(w^k\bigr)w^{k-1} \mathrm{d} w & -\phi_0\bigl(w^k\bigr) w^{k-1} \mathrm{d} w \end{pmatrix},
 \end{align}
 where $w$ is a coordinate centered at $x$, such that $\check{p}\colon w \mapsto z=w^k$. By assumption, $k=2,3$. The pullback quasi-parabolic structure is given by $\mathcal{E}'_{x,1}=\langle \check{p}^*s_1 \: \rule[-3.5pt]{0.5pt}{11.5pt}\,{}_y\rangle$. Now, it is an easy computation to see that the Hecke modification modifies the Higgs field to
 \[ \hat{\Phi} = \begin{pmatrix} \phi_0\bigl(w^k\bigr) w^{k-1} \mathrm{d} w & \phi_1\bigl(w^k\bigr) \mathrm{d} w \\[1mm] \phi_2\bigl(w^k\bigr)w^{k-2} \mathrm{d} w & -\phi_0\bigl(w^k\bigr) w^{k-1} \mathrm{d} w \end{pmatrix}.
 \]
 Hence, indeed $(\hat{\mathcal{E}},\hat{\Phi})$ defines a $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})$-Higgs bundle. Its polystability will follow from the existence of a solution to Hitchin's equation at the end of the proof.

 \textit{Hitchin sections:} Now, we want to apply this morphism to a point in the Hitchin section. We~identify the Hitchin base of $\mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$ as $\{ c \eta \mid c \in \mathbb{C}\}$ for a fixed quadratic differential $\eta$ with simple poles at~$D$. Denote by $q=\check{p}^*\eta$ its pullback. Then a point $(\mathcal{E},\Phi)$ in the Hitchin section of $\mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$ is given by
 \[ (\mathcal{E},\Phi)=\left( \mathcal{O}(-1) \oplus \mathcal{O}(-3), \begin{pmatrix} 0 & c \\ \eta & 0 \end{pmatrix} \right) \in \mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}.
 \]
 After pullback and tensoring, we obtain
 \[ (\mathcal{E}',\Phi')=\left( K^{\frac12}(R_1+R_2) \oplus K^{-\frac12}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 & c \check{p}^*1 \\ \check{p}^* \eta & 0 \end{pmatrix} \right).
 \]
 Here $\check{p}^*1 \in \check{p}^*\mathcal{O}(2) \otimes \check{p}^*K_{\mathbb{P}^1}$ has a zero of order $1$ at each $2:1$ ramification point and a zero of order $2$ at each $3:1$ ramification point. The pullback quasi-parabolic structure at $\check{p}^{-1}D$ is given by the second coordinate with respect to the splitting. Hence, the Hecke modification yields
 \[ \Theta(\mathcal{E},\Phi)=\left( K^{\frac12} \oplus K^{-\frac12}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 & cq \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \right)=s_H(cq)
 \]
 as asserted.

 \textit{Compatibility with pullback by $p$:} We show that this map extends the spectral correspondence on the regular locus. First we showed above that the Hitchin section of $\mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$ is mapped on~the Hitchin section of $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X)$. It is easy to see that the eigen-line bundle on $E$ of the Hitchin section of $\mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$ is $\check{\pi}^*\mathcal{O}(-3)$. Similarly, the eigen-line bundle on $\Sigma$ of the Hitchin section of~$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X)$ is~\smash{$\pi^*K_X^{-\frac12}$}. We use these two Hitchin sections to identify the fibers with the corresponding abelian varieties. Then $(\mathcal{E},\Phi) \in \mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$ corresponds to an element $L_1 \in \mathrm{Jac}(E)$. Similarly, $\bigl(\hat{\mathcal{E}},\hat{\Phi}\bigr)$ corresponds to an element $L_2 \in \mathrm{Prym}(\Sigma_q)$. We need to show that $L_2=p^*L_1$. From the spectral correspondence, we have an exact sequence
 \[ 0 \rightarrow L_1 \otimes \check{\pi}^*\mathcal{O}(-3) \rightarrow \check{\pi}^*\mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\check{\pi}^*\Phi-\omega \mathrm{id}_{\check{\pi}^* \mathcal{E}}} \check{\pi}^* (\mathcal{E} \otimes \mathcal{O}(2) ).
 \]
 Tensoring with $\mathcal{O}(3)$ and pulling back, we obtain
 \[ 0 \rightarrow p^*L_1 \rightarrow \pi^*\bigl(\mathcal{E}' \otimes K_X^{\frac12}\bigr) \xrightarrow{\pi^*\Phi'-\lambda \mathrm{id}_{\check{\pi}^* \mathcal{E}}} \pi^*\bigl(\mathcal{E}' \otimes K_X^{\frac12}\bigr) \otimes (\check{\pi} \circ p)^*\mathcal{O}(2).
 \]
 Here we used the commutativity of diagram in Figure~\ref{fig:square-of-covers}.
 Finally, twisting by \smash{$K_X^{-\frac12}$} we see that the line bundle associated to $\pi^*(\mathcal{E}',\Phi')$ through the spectral correspondence is $p^*L_1$. The (pullback of the) Hecke modification $\hat{\mathcal{E}} \rightarrow \mathcal{E}$ can potentially change this line bundle by twisting it with a~divisor supported at~$\pi^{-1}R$. However, on the regular locus of $\mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$ the quasi-parabolic structure is uniquely determined through the Higgs field at each $p \in D$ (see \cite[Proposition~8.1]{FMSW}). Hence, we can compute the eigen-line bundle and the quasi-parabolic structure of $\pi^*(\mathcal{E}',\Phi')$ with respect to the pullback of the local frame of~\eqref{eq:local-model-Phi}. Then it is easy to see that the eigen-line bundle \smash{$p^*L_1 \otimes K_x^{-\frac12}$} descends to a subbundle of $\pi^*(\hat{\mathcal{E}},\hat{\Phi})$. Hence $p^*L_1=L_2$.


 \textit{Solutions to Hitchin equation:} Finally, we will show that a hermitian metric $h$ on ${(\mathcal{E},\Phi) \in \mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}}$ that solves the Hitchin equation is transformed to a solution to the Hitchin equation for $\bigl(\hat{\mathcal{E}},\hat{\Phi}\bigr) \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X)$. First there is a section of $\mathcal{O}(4)$ with divisors $D$. Promoting this section to have norm $1$ defines a singular hermitian metric on~$\mathcal{O}(4)$ locally given by $\vert z \vert^{-2}$ at $y \in D$. This induces a singular hermitian metric on $\mathcal{O}(1)$ and hence on $\mathcal{O}(3)$. The latter is given by \smash{$\vert z \vert ^{-\frac32}$} at $y \in D$ and will be denoted by~$h_{\mathcal{O}(3)}$. Similarly, $q \in H^0\bigl(X,K_X^2\bigr)$ induces a singular hermitian metric \smash{$h_{-\frac12 K_X}$} on \smash{$K_X^{-\frac 12}$} that is smooth away from $Z(q)$ and given by \smash{$\vert w \vert^{\frac12}$} locally at $x \in Z(q)$. It is easy to see that singular hermitian metrics defined in this way are automatically flat.

 We need to extend the morphism $\Theta$ to hermitian Higgs bundles $(\mathcal{E},\Phi,h)$. In the first step, we use the singular hermitian metrics defined above to obtain a hermitian metric on $\mathcal{E}'$ by
 \[ (\mathcal{E}',h')=\pi^* ((E,h) \otimes (\mathcal{O}(3),h_{\mathcal{O}(3)}) ) \otimes \bigl(K_X^{-\frac12},h_{-\frac12 K_X}\bigr).
 \]
 This hermitian metric is holomorphic on $X\setminus R$. The hermitian metric~$h'$ pulls back to a hermitian metric $\hat{h}$ on $\mathcal{E}$ through the Hecke modification $\hat{\mathcal{E}} \rightarrow \mathcal{E}$ a priori holomorphic only on $X \setminus R$.

 Now, we start with a polystable Higgs bundle $(\mathcal{E},\Phi) \in \mathcal{M}_{\alpha}$ and let $h$ be a solution to Hitchin's equation. By the flatness of the hermitian metrics $h_{\mathcal{O}(3)}$ and \smash{$h_{-\frac12 K_X}$}, the resulting hermitian metric~$h'$ on $\mathcal{E}$ will still be a solution to Hitchin's equation wherever it is smooth. By definition, the Hecke modification $\hat{\mathcal{E}} \rightarrow \mathcal{E}$ is an isomorphism on $X \setminus R$ and hence the induced metric~$\hat{h}$ is a solution to Hitchin's equation on this locus. To show that it defines a solution to Hitchin's equation on~$X$, we are left with showing that it extends smoothly over~$R$.

 To do so, we compute the local description of $\hat{h}$ at $x \in R$. The metric $h$ is adapted to the parabolic structure. Hence, at $y \in D$ we can find a local frame $s_1$, $s_2$ of $\mathcal{E}$ such that firstly
 \[ h= \begin{pmatrix} \vert z \vert^{2\alpha_1} & \\ & \vert z \vert^{2\alpha_2} \end{pmatrix},
 \]
 secondly the Higgs field is given by \eqref{eq:local-model-Phi} and thirdly the quasi-parabolic structure is the ascending flag $\langle s_1 \rangle \subset \langle s_1,s_2 \rangle$. We have to consider two cases depending on the ramification index of the fiber over $y \in D$. We will only give the details for $y \in D$ of ramification index~$2$, i.e., $\check{p}^{-1}y$ is made up from $3:1$ ramification points.

 In this case, the compatible parabolic weight are \smash{$\underline{\alpha}_y=\bigl(\frac34, \frac14\bigr)$}, so that \smash{$h=\mathrm{diag}\bigl( \vert z \vert^{\frac{4}{3}}, \vert z \vert^{\frac{2}{3}}\bigr)$}. Tensoring with $(\mathcal{O}(3),h_{\mathcal{O}(3)})$, pulling back and then tensoring with \smash{$\bigl(K_X^{-\frac12},h_{-\frac12 K}\bigr)$}, we obtain a~local description for $h'$ at $x \in Z(q)$ with respect to the induced frame
 \[ h'= \check{p}^*\mathrm{diag}\bigl( \vert z \vert^{\frac{4}{3}-\frac32}, \vert z \vert^{\frac{2}{3}-\frac32}\bigr) \vert w \vert^{\frac12}= \mathrm{diag}\bigl( 1, \vert w \vert^{-2} \bigr).
 \]
 Here $w$ is local coordinate at $x \in \check{p}^{-1}y$, such that $\check{p}\colon w \mapsto w^3=z$. Finally, with respect to the frame $s_1$, $s_2$ the Hecke modification $\hat{\mathcal{E}} \rightarrow \mathcal{E}$ is given by $\mathrm{diag}( 1, w)$ and hence the induced metric on $\hat{\mathcal{E}}$ is indeed smooth at $x \in R$ of ramification index~$2$. The case of ramification index~$1$ follows along the same lines. Hence, $\hat{h}$ defines a smooth solution to the Hitchin equation for the Higgs bundle $\bigl(\hat{\mathcal{E}},\hat{\Phi}\bigr)$.

 In particular, for a polystable Higgs bundle $(\mathcal{E},\Phi) \in \mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}$ the image $\Theta(\mathcal{E},\Phi)$ is polystable and hence indeed $\Theta$ defines a map of moduli spaces
 \[ \Theta\colon \ \mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}} \rightarrow \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X).
 \]
 This finishes the proof.

title: Corollary
body_md: \label{coro:hyperholomorphic} Let $(X,q)$ be a uniform pillowcase cover. Then $\mathcal{I}_q \subset \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{PGL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X)$ is a hyperholomorphic subvariety.
head: environment

title: \proofname
body_md: By Theorem~\ref{theo:Theta}, $\Theta$ maps solutions to the Hitchin equation on $\bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,D\bigr)$ to solutions to the Hitchin equation on~$X$. Hence, it is holomorphic not only with respect to the holomorphic structure~$I$, but also with respect to the holomorphic structure~$J$ and~$K$ on the moduli spaces $\mathcal{M}_{\underline{\alpha}}\bigl(\mathbb{P}^1,D\bigr)$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})}(X)$. In particular, its image is a hyperholomorphic subvariety.
